items.title: Why neutrality is worth chasing, even if no one gets there
items.summary: Critics say neutrality is impossible, but Jimmy Wales, founder of Wikipedia and author of The Seven Rules of Trust , argues that this is no reason to stop trying. In this conversation with Jonny Thomson, he explains why a fight over a single word, from “Gdańsk” to “security fence,” is often what an encyclopedia should explain. He also says no one can fully see the biases built into AI models, and that people were cruel to each other online long before algorithms. The two also discuss why Wales won’t put money into Wikipedia editing and where editorial judgment ends and censorship begins. They close with his optimistic view of the next 20 years. This video Why neutrality is worth chasing, even if no one gets there is featured on Big Think .

items.title: Ease productivity overload with “niksen,” the Dutch art of doing nothing
items.summary: When was the last time you did nothing? By that, I don’t mean scrolling through social media, mowing the lawn, or fretting over the latest office drama. I mean a do-nothingness with no purpose and no goal other than to just enjoy being. If you’re like most modern adults, you’ll likely have trouble recalling such a luxurious moment, and even if you could, would you openly admit it? The more you think about it, the more you realize how incredibly difficult it is not only to find the time for nothing but to own it without embarrassment. In our work- and improvement-focused culture, doing nothing isn’t the mark of time well-spent . Check the dictionary, and you won’t find a positive-sounding label for a do-nothing. You will, however, discover a buffet of labels that discourage the very idea, with all the disappointment of a finger-wagging grandpa: deadbeat , laggard , lazybones , loafer , slacker , couch potato , and lotus eater . Little wonder then that we fill our schedules with work, activities, and chores under the pressure to constantly produce — even if such busywork is for the sake of performance. But English may finally have a word that captures not only the joys of unoccupied moments but also the benefits they can bring. It’s niksen , and it’s on loan from the Netherlands. Rebranding niksen In its native Dutch, niksen means literally “to do nothing.” According to Maartje Williems, author of The Lost Art of Doing Nothing , the verb comes from the noun niks (nothing), and it wasn’t coined to be a ringing endorsement. This is evidenced by its lexical cousin niksnut — essentially, a layabout who does nothing and doesn’t contribute to society. (The Netherlands has its share of finger-wagging grandpas, too.) But in the last decade, niksen has undergone a rebranding . In 2017, journalist Gebke Verhoeven published an article titled “Niksen Is the New Mindfulness” in the magazine Gezond Nu (Healthy Now). The article applied the Dutch verb to the benefits of relaxation that psychologists and sociologists were seeing in their research. As Verhoeven wrote: “We cram our free time so that we don’t have a minute left to just do nothing. Is that bad? Yes, that’s bad. You don’t give your brain space and time to process information and feel what you really need. In short, you lose yourself a bit. High time to elevate idleness to art.” Your few days together have been spent doing nothing really, which is something, is an intimacy in itself. Caleb Azumah Nelson The article inspired other journalists to explore the research under the label of niksen too — among them Olga Mecking, who wrote a popular piece on the subject for The New York Times . As if by providence, many of these articles came out in 2019, just before the COVID-19 pandemic abruptly forced people to reconsider how they spend their idle time. For the record, Dutch isn’t the first language to coin a term for the splendor of laziness. Italian, for example, has the tasty expression la dolce far niente (literally, “sweet doing nothing”). It doesn’t get as much play today, as it sounds a bit dated and cliched to modern ears. The expression did, however, serve as the inspiration for several works of art, including a series of oil paintings by Neoclassicist John William Godward. But it seems niksen — admittedly more compact — has gained widespread acceptance as the word to represent the concept today. John William Godward wasn’t alone in portraying 19th-century niksen . This 1880 oil painting by John William Waterhouse is also titled La Dolce Far Niente . It seems doing sweet nothing was a popular idea at the time. (Credit: Wikimedia Commons) How does one practice niksen? To niksen, you only need to be idle for a time without trying to be productive or fulfill a purpose. That’s it. It sounds as easy as curling up in your favorite chair. Yet in practice, it’s far more difficult. Imagine you work remotely, and you take a break to clean out the dishwasher. Is that niksen? No. You’re using your time to be productive, and that’s not doing nothing. What about scrolling through your Instagram feed instead? Again, no. You’ve used the time to catch up with all the online happenings. Even if you sit doing nothing, your mind can betray your endeavors. Spending the time planning out an upcoming presentation means you’re still at work. And despite the title of Verhoeven’s 2017 article, mindfulness isn’t niksen either . Mindfulness has the explicit goal of being fully present in the moment. Meanwhile, niksen’s purpose-free musings are more akin to mindlessness. It is awfully hard work doing nothing. Oscar Wilde So what does count? Staring out the window and watching birds flit around. Enjoying the aroma of your coffee as it brews in the morning. Having a pleasant daydream as music plays in the background. Sitting in a cafe and watching the people pass by. It’s any “unguarded moment,” Williems writes, of “having nothing to do and not finding something new to do.” Beyond that, there are no hard-and-fast rules. Williems recommends the moments be spontaneous, have no time limit, and be in a distraction-free environment. But Carolien Hamming, managing director of CSR Centrum, a stress coaching center, advises you to schedule sessions and use a timer, especially if you’re just starting out. Some even suggest incorporating an easygoing activity with no specific goal. Think walking , knitting, pen spinning, or brewing a cup of tea. “Dare to be idle,” Hamming told TIME . “It is all about allowing life to run its course, and to free us from obligations for just a moment.” The benefits of being a do-nothing I am unaware of any studies that have specifically looked at niksen as detailed above. The concept is likely too new and amorphous. We’ll have to wait and see. That said, much research points to the benefits of rest and relaxation, and niksen could offer similar benefits for people who find the practice checks both boxes. One such benefit is improved focus and decision-making. Your frontal lobe — a section of the brain involved in decision-making and self-control — grows fatigued the more cognitive load is put on it. When you rest, your frontal lobe throttles down and lets your default mode network take over. This different brain state reduces the cognitive load, so your frontal lobe has more energy when you return to your daily to-dos. While your brain revives most during sleep, research shows that resting throughout the day can boost your mental performance. As Emily Maloney wrote about her niksen experience for The Washington Post : “These breaks in my day were most helpful when I was tired and needed a reset, when I was looking for space to be creative, or when I was having trouble focusing on a task I needed to do. Instead of fighting my natural rhythms, I gave in to them.” Cognitive load can also explain why breaks that include chores, social media scrolling, and the like aren’t as effective. Rather than letting your frontal lobe wind down, they thrust a whole new set of decisions and self-control challenges at it. Don’t underestimate the value of doing nothing, of just going along, listening to all the things you can’t hear, and not bothering. A.A. Milne Meaningful breaks have been shown to help reduce stress , too. While some stress can motivate you to accomplish a task or rise to a challenge, too much stress or stress held for too long can harm your performance and productivity. It isn’t great for your health and well-being either. By building relaxing moments into your days, you can better balance your stress levels by tapping into your “rest-and-digest” response (the counterpart to the more famous “fight-or-flight” response). items.title: The universe built its own telescope out of space and time
items.summary: When you see the sun, you’re seeing it as it was eight minutes ago. When you see the Andromeda galaxy, the light reaching your eyes left 2.5 million years ago. Astronomer Michelle Thaller, who spent 28 years at NASA, explains why everyone who looks at the sky is looking back in time. She also explains how today’s telescopes can now see the universe as it was more than 12 billion years ago. This video The universe built its own telescope out of space and time is featured on Big Think .

items.title: He Thought About Rome Every Day
items.summary: The year was 1764, and Edward Gibbon was 27, headed for Rome on his Grand Tour. He had traversed the Alps from France not on a mule but in a chair carried between poles by porters. (He was “no great jockey,” a companion noted.) Gibbon then made his way through Turin and Milan, paused in Florence, and, as autumn set in, continued south. Crossing the Tiber, his destination now in sight, he was overcome. “I can neither express nor forget the strong emotions which agitated my mind as I first approached and entered the eternal city,” Gibbon recalled years later in a memoir. “After a sleepless night I trod, with a lofty step, the ruins of the Forum; each memorable spot where Romulus stood or Tully spoke or Caesar fell was at once present to my eye; and several days of intoxication were lost or enjoyed before I could descend to a cool and minute investigation.” Gibbon loved his rhetorical couplings—those harnessed pairs of verbs or adjectives that are sometimes at odds (“lost or enjoyed,” “express nor forget”), pulling the reader in different directions, as the critic Clive James once observed . The oddest pairing of all is that of Gibbon himself and his monumental work, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire , which he began writing seven years after that first (and only) visit to Rome. Gibbon was, by his own description, “puny”—4 feet 7 inches tall. His masterpiece is towering, a million and a half words published over the course of little more than a decade. The first of the six volumes—an immediate best seller in Britain—appeared the same year as the Declaration of Independence and The Wealth of Nations . There was no real precedent for what Gibbon had achieved. The Decline and Fall was an attempt to write history in a way we now take for granted : that is, by seeking to explain what actually happened. Gibbon was neither an annalist nor a zealot. He had arguments to make—about the unrivaled stability and happiness enjoyed for a spell by the Roman empire’s subjects, about the defeat of liberty by despotism and decadence, about the corrosive effects of corruption and Christianity—but his account is not subservient to them. He is often imprecise, as well as confident in his imagination. But he also weighs evidence. He compares cultures. He shifts perspective. Gibbon’s appetite for written sources was gargantuan and his knowledge of them profound, though he did not bring a modern critical faculty to their interpretation. He was an impresario, not a pedant—judicious, skeptical, and ironic, with a taste for drama. And the writing! At times so over-egged as to make Henry James seem like Hemingway, but seductive in its rhythms and illuminated by epigrammatic flashes: “A good soldier should dread his own officers far more than the enemy.” “Revenge is profitable, gratitude is expensive.” The narrative is at once sweeping and detailed—equal parts Balzac and Trollope, George Lucas and TMZ. The Decline and Fall ’s influence has been immense. The work created the basic storyline of Roman history , from “good emperors” to barbarians, and for generations has shaped an understanding of imperial ruin as “the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness.” It captivated newly independent America, whose Founders cherished republican government but feared that the Roman past held danger signs. People continue to explore its claims and insights, as well as the experiences that shaped its author: Was Gibbon a fatalist or, living at the core of a young empire himself , an optimist? Whatever the answer, his eyes seem to follow us around the room. Gibbon the man is a figure, as Martha Saxton writes in her posthumously published The Conversions of Edward Gibbon: A Modern Biography , who appears almost laughably devoid of the majesty his prose leads you to expect. As a boy, his ungainly body and unhappy experiences with peers left him deeply insecure and drove him to books. In later life, he grew obese and suffered from a hydrocele—a scrotal swelling—that further hampered his movement. He was vain and foppish, with a habit of waving his snuffbox didactically when he wanted to make a point. People acknowledged his brilliance but also made him an object of ridicule and even contempt. James Boswell, who knew Gibbon as a member of the Club, a literary group that included Samuel Johnson, described him as an “ugly, affected, disgusting fellow.” Saxton, a feminist historian and for many years a professor at Amherst College, is the author of acclaimed biographies of Jayne Mansfield, Louisa May Alcott, and Mary Ball Washington (the mother of George). She came to Gibbon from an unusual angle, her attention drawn initially by the notable misogyny of the Decline and Fall . Powerful women are painted as gorgons or succubi. The few whom Gibbon approves of are described as possessing “manly” virtues. In Gibbon’s lexicon, decadence is often a synonym for effeminacy . But Saxton’s response to Gibbon is complicated. She describes herself as both repelled by his venom and dazzled by the Decline and Fall —by its writing, scope, and command, and by the mark it left. She also finds Gibbon’s misogyny baffling. Male writers of the Enlightenment were eager to engage a female audience. Gibbon himself enjoyed close friendships with several women, in particular an aunt, Catherine Porten, who first cultivated “a taste for books, which is still the pleasure and glory of my life.” Aunt Kitty would be Gibbon’s friend and counselor for nearly four decades. Saxton doesn’t have a ready explanation for Gibbon’s attitudes, and doesn’t try to force one. Instead, she broadens her inquiry to explore the inner life of a man who repeatedly broke with convention—the “conversions” of her title—only to scramble back to safer ground. A lonely misfit emerges from her book, confident in his abilities but wounded in his soul, who escapes into a world of words as the only place where he can exercise complete control. Saxton is hardly protective of her subject, but she also has no patience for the cruelty of men like Boswell, whose remarks about Gibbon give her “much sympathy for the tiny, affected, brilliant, scarred man.” [ From the January 1878 issue: William Dean Howells on Edward Gibbon ] Gibbon was born in South London in 1737 to a family of wealth and property. Though sickly himself, he was the only one of seven children to survive infancy. His unloving mother died when he was 10. His difficult father was a stern traditionalist who kept a tight hold on money and behavior. Young Edward was sent away for schooling. The most significant event from Gibbon’s brief time at Oxford was his rebellious embrace of Catholicism—not a route to advancement in 18th-century Britain. He was sent to stay with a Calvinist pastor and his family in Lausanne, Switzerland. The prospect of disinheritance proved to be a potent theology. As Gibbon later wrote, “The various articles of the Romish creed disappeared like a dream.” But the five years spent in Lausanne also made him a French-speaking child of the Enlightenment, with continental manners and republican values. He took inspiration from the Swiss fight for democracy—a movement, he once wrote, from which “the dullest stranger would catch fire.” He acquired habits of reading and study that he never relinquished. Lausanne was also where he met an intellectually intrepid young woman named Suzanne Curchod and embarked on the one romantic adventure of his life. But his father refused to bless their engagement—Suzanne had no wealth and no desire to live in England—and Gibbon broke it off. “I sighed as a lover,” he recalled years later. “I obeyed as a son.” In fact, he did more than obey. Returning home, he made a kind of peace with his father, slipped into a caricature of Englishness, and adopted the macho swagger of his class. items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Novels of 2026
items.summary: It’s been, in my opinion, an excellent year for novels. So excellent that this list was exceedingly hard to whittle down. We had long-awaited books from beloved authors like Marlon James, Min Jin Lee, and Ben Lerner—occupying vastly opposite ends of the page-count spectrum—and countless exciting debuts. But what’s thrilled me most about all the books I’ve read this year is how strange, distinct, and utterly human they are. I’ve expounded before on the value of literature in the age of AI, but we are another year deeper into its all-too-rapid encroachment on our art, so you’ll have to forgive me for getting up on my soapbox once again. As em-dashes are being described as a hallmark of AI-writing rather than as a writer’s favorite punctuation mark to overuse, now co-opted by the machines who stole from us, I’ve found myself asking: What, exactly, makes art human ? If we are being asked to rethink even our grammar choices so as not to be mistaken for robots, how do we make art that is profoundly and undeniably our own? I can’t say whether or not the authors on this list were writing with this question in mind, but I can say for certain that for me, their books are answering it. Our favorite books of 2026 got weird , in every sense of the word. They got creative on a line-level, on a structure-level, on a content-level. They are utterly distinct in their voice and style, from Scott McClanahan’s Fights! to the numerous narrators of The Disappearers , each instantly identifiable by voice. Some grapple with existential questions about our technological age more directly: Ben Lerner entangles our modern digital-reliance with questions of memory; in Earth 7 , it’s unclear whether a love interest is or is not a robot; Attention-Seeking Behavior questions the nature of truth. Last year, in an editorial meeting, several of my colleagues and I were wondering what would happen to literature as AI became bigger, louder, and more insistent on its presence in our daily lives, whether we want it or not (and if the recent blue tsunami votes on data centers are any indication, the overall consensus is not ). The one silver lining I could find was the hope that it might embolden writers to be weirder. More distinct. More themselves. Less afraid. If the books on this list are any indication, writers are doing exactly that. My hope now is that each of these beautiful, varied, dynamic works might remind you of what it means to be human. –Katie Henken Robinson Deputy Editor Editor’s note: The following books were hand-selected by Electric Literature staff and interns, with the help of our community of contributors, readers, and friends of the organization. While books by current staff or board members are not eligible for consideration, we would like to informally recommend The True Confessions of First Lady Freeman by board member Deesha Philyaw, another novel we loved this year! The 10 titles below are presented alphabetically by title; they are not ranked. Afternoon Hours of a Hermit by Patrick Cottrell In Afternoon Hours of a Hermit , Patrick Cottrell’s deeply moving and utterly arresting second novel, Dan Moran, a transmasculine Korean adoptee returns home on the eve of his dead brother’s memorial dinner. Estranged from his family, he embarks on a search in the wake of his brother’s death: he searches for the women who knew him, acting as a detective, longing to better understand how his younger brother understood him. Heartbreaking, absurd, and incredibly intimate, this novel will leave you questioning everything you thought you knew about yourself, about making art, about the world. – Denne Michele Norris , Executive Director and Publisher Attention-Seeking Behavior by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo I’ve been thinking a lot about the line between fact and fiction. I notice the blur of its movement in every social media post, I see its oscillation in the big blue eyes of Elizabeth Holmes, in the collective fictions that move the stock market. The question of what is true—or, maybe, the question of what is truth —is the white-hot center of Aea Varfis-van Warmelo’s debut Attention-Seeking Behavior . The novel’s narrator is a young woman living in London. Her story opens with a direct address: “You should know,” followed by a confession: “when I found the body I did not scream.” It’s a killer first line and a disturbing first scene —in it, the narrator also admits to feigning humanity when reporting the body, to finding the death immaculately beautiful, and to eating a croissant immediately after her discovery. Perhaps more disturbing, the scene ends in an acknowledgement: “There is no way to prove that it happened, but why would I lie?” Of course, asking the question is itself slightly suspect, but it queues the novel up perfectly. If it’s a question you’re interested in pressing against, you’ll find no better place. – Wynter K Miller , Director of Operations and Fiction Editor Earth 7 by Deb Olin Unferth Even in the strangest of circumstances, love persists. Even if you’re (possibly) a robot and an ocean-pod-raised woman meeting on an artificial beach. But Earth 7 is so much more than a love story; Deb Olin Unferth is interested in big questions, such as why we love at all, and what drives us to keep living no matter the state of the world. Embracing the strangeness of speculative fiction in order to get at the heart of what makes us most human, this novel packs an outsized philosophical punch for its slim size. It may be just the book we need as the climate crisis only grows in scope. –Rachel Maybee , Editorial Intern Famous Men by Julie Buntin Julie Buntin interrogates the seductive pull of literary lineage in Famous Men . Growing up in small-town Michigan, Wilhemina “Will” Miles devours the work of celebrated author Nathaniel Fellow, suspecting he might be her biological father. When she moves to New York and becomes his assistant and student, their boundary-blurring dynamic tangles creative ambition with desire and dependency. Throughout the novel, Buntin traces the way power disguises itself as taste, mentorship, and artistic rigor, leaving Will to confront the fact that the voice which inspired her to imagine a life devoted to writing is inextricable from harm. That tension makes the novel gripping, and Bunton shows with remarkable clarity how the desire for a literary life can feel as intimate and dangerous as love. – Shandela Contreras , Editorial Intern Fights! by Scott McClanahan I have without a doubt recommended Fights! to more people than any other novel this year. Fights! is a kind of miracle book. It’s weighty, but if you catch its wave, you’ll read it in a night. It’s about publishing books in NYC and West Virginia in the 2010s; it’s also about loving people, working and being unable to work with people you love, and finding a way to sustain love even when a relationship collapses, a person dies, a life changes. McClanahan’s language has a subtle way of folding itself around the reader. As I read Fights! for the first time over the course of a long night, anecdotes, stories, emotions—all a far cry from my life—seemed to become my own in the most unexpected and intimate ways. McClanahan wrote a list for EL about stealing from other writers while he wrote Fights! , but for the life of me, this is among the most personal and honest novels I’ve read. I’d love to know how McClanahan manages to steal and tell the truth so well. – Willem Marx , Associate Editor Honey in the Wound by Jiyoung Han This multi-generational epic, which approaches the tragedy of “comfort women”—women forced into sexual slavery by Japanese imperialism—with empathy and grace, sets a high bar for a debut novel. Jiyoung Han has earned her place in the must-read canon of magical realism, right alongside classics like One Hundred Years of Solitude . items.title: 3 keys will unlock the next level in how the Universe began
items.summary: In all the Universe, there’s no bigger question — and no greater mystery — than where all of this came from, and how all of this came to be. For countless generations, our cosmic origins were a question for poets, theologians, and philosophers, as our scientific knowledge had not yet advanced to the point where we could uncover an evidence-based answer to such questions. However, the 20th and 21st centuries changed all of that, allowing us to pin down the answers to such questions as: What rules govern our Universe? What is the Universe made of? How large and how old is it? How did it come to be the way it is today? And what are our ultimate cosmic origins? We often say, now, that our Universe began with the hot Big Bang, but that’s only the Universe as we know and experience it today: the observable Universe. We’ve since learned that the Big Bang itself was preceded and set up by an earlier phase in cosmic history: cosmic inflation , where space itself contained an enormous amount of inherent energy and expanded — or inflated — rapidly and relentlessly. When inflation ended, our hot Big Bang ensued, giving rise to the Universe as we know, observe, and exist within it. But what, exactly, were inflation’s properties? What type of inflation occurred, and what relics, or imprints, of inflation remain within our observable Universe today? Although we’ve come remarkably far in our understanding of our cosmic origins, there are a few windows still left unexplored that can take our understanding to the next level. Here are the three big ones where new data will help guide the way. Our Universe, from the hot Big Bang until the present day, underwent a huge amount of growth and evolution, and continues to do so. Our entire observable Universe was approximately the size of a modest boulder some 13.8 billion years ago, but it has expanded to be ~46 billion light-years in radius today. The complex structure that has arisen must have grown from seed imperfections of at least ~0.003% of the average density early on, and has gone through phases where atomic nuclei, neutral atoms, and stars first formed, eventually giving rise to our Solar System, planet, life, and humans. Credit : NASA/CXC/M. Weiss We truly went from not knowing what the Universe was, at all, to figuring out an enormous amount about our cosmic origins in the span of less than 150 years. Our journey began in earnest in the late 19th century, when people began to notice breakdowns in Newtonian mechanics at speeds close to the speed of light, and hints of a breakdown in Newtonian gravity when it came to the orbit of the planet Mercury. Both of those puzzles were eventually resolved with Einstein and relativity: special relativity for Newtonian mechanics, and general relativity, incorporating gravity in a relativistic framework, to eventually resolve the precession of Mercury’s perihelion. Within that new framework for gravity, several new exact solutions emerged. These included the: Minkowski solution, which reduces to flat, uncurved, matter-free space, Schwarzschild solution, for a non-rotating black hole, de Sitter solution, for a Universe dominated by a cosmological constant, and Friedmann solution, for a Universe that was both isotropic (the same in all directions) and homogeneous (the same in all locations) and filled evenly with at least one form of energy. Friedmann’s solution, derived in 1922, was particularly interesting from a cosmic perspective, because it showed that static spacetimes that were uniformly filled with “stuff” were unstable; the Universe must expand or contract. A plot of the apparent expansion rate (y-axis) vs. distance (x-axis) is consistent with a Universe that expanded faster in the past, but where distant galaxies are accelerating in their recession today. This is a modern version of, extending thousands of times farther than, Hubble’s original work. Note the fact that the points do not form a straight line, indicating the expansion rate’s change over time. The fact that the Universe follows the curve it does is indicative of the presence, and late-time dominance, of dark energy. Credit : Ned Wright/Betoule et al., 2014 Contemporaneously, starting in 1923, we began identifying individual stars within the spiral and elliptical nebulae in the skies: determining that they were galaxies beyond the Milky Way. When we combined those distance measurements with redshift measurements, or how fast these galaxies appeared to recede from us, we found a relationship: the farther the galaxy, the faster the recession speed. When this relationship was placed into the context of Friedmann’s solution, we arrived at the expanding Universe: the first big step toward understanding our cosmic origins. If the Universe is expanding today, then that means things are getting farther apart, becoming less dense, and — since the wavelength of radiation is stretching to become longer — cooling as well. If things are getting less dense and cooling today, that means that they were denser and hotter in the past. Since gravitation attracts objects and brings them together, the Universe should become more structure rich, i.e., clumpier, as time goes on as well. Therefore, this points toward an early state of the Universe that was hotter, denser, and more uniform than it is today. At the start of the hot Big Bang, the Universe was rapidly expanding and filled with high-energy, very densely packed, ultra-relativistic quanta. An early stage of radiation domination gave way to several later stages where radiation was sub-dominant, but never went away completely, while matter then clumped into gas clouds, stars, star clusters, galaxies, and even richer structures over time, all while the Universe continues expanding. The expansion rate evolves dependent on the sum total of all the forms of energy present within it, linking the observed expansion to the energy contents of our cosmos. Credit: Big Think / Ben Gibson / NASA / Pablo Carlos Budassi If you start off with a very hot, very dense, very uniform, and rapidly expanding Universe, then as time goes on, the following sets of things will occur. Particles will clump together, forming protons and neutrons, and then protons and neutrons will fuse together into atomic nuclei: creating an initial set of elements even before stars have formed. Atomic nuclei and electrons will combine together, and as the Universe cools sufficiently to make stable, neutral atoms, any photons (or radiation) that was present back then will simply stream outward in a straight line, stretching in wavelength and cooling as the Universe expands to create a persistent background of radiation: the CMB. Gravitation will pull matter together into clumps: creating stars, star clusters, small galaxies, larger galaxies, groups and clusters of galaxies, and even grander structures akin to a cosmic web. As time goes on, this web-like structure gets more well-defined and more pronounced. And the Universe keeps on expanding, with the expansion rate changing as the density of the Universe changes, resulting in a particular relationship between the expansion rate over time and the matter-and-energy contents of the Universe. These are the four cornerstones of the hot Big Bang, and all four have been observationally confirmed. In the top panel, our modern Universe has the same properties (including temperature) everywhere because they originated from a region possessing the same properties. In the middle panel, the space that could have had any arbitrary curvature is inflated to the point where we cannot observe any curvature today, solving the flatness problem. And in the bottom panel, pre-existing high-energy relics are inflated away, providing a solution to the high-energy relic problem. This is how inflation solves the three great puzzles that the Big Bang cannot account for on its own. Credit : E. Siegel/Beyond the Galaxy Howe
